title: Pushing it: resonance, and reading a model

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the dots on the graph of swing against frequency climbing to a peak near 2 rad/s, where the spring and mass forces cancel, when you drag the drive frequency.
interactive.title: The driven swing
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson in twelve small screens. It uses the same spring as before. A 1 kg mass sits on a 4 N/m spring, with a 0.5 N·s/m damper. Now a push of 1 N swings back and forth as F cos ωt. Here ω is how fast the push swings, in rad/s. Screen 1 shows the mass with the push arrow beside it, growing and shrinking. Under it is the rule m x″ + c x′ + k x = F cos ωt. Each term is labelled as a force in newtons. A trace shows position over 30 s, from −1.2 to 1.2 m. It starts from rest at 0, with the push at 1 rad/s. Play runs it. Its read sentence: the trace starts lumpy because the spring's own ringing mixes in, then settles to an even swing by about 20 s. A faint envelope shows the ringing dying, with a 4 s time constant. Screen 2 asks how often it swings once it has settled. One choice is 1 rad/s, the push's rate. Another is about 2 rad/s, its own ringing rate. The third is 1.5 rad/s, halfway. The answer is 1 rad/s. The ringing is the transient, and it dies. Screen 3 draws the three force arrows of the steady swing, end to end. The spring's pull kX points one way. The mass term mω²X points the opposite way, because two derivatives of a cosine give −ω² times it. The damper's drag cωX is at right angles. Together they make the 1 N push. A drive slider runs from 0.25 to 4 rad/s in steps of 0.25. It opens at 1. At 1 rad/s the swing is 0.329 m. The arrows are then 1.32 N, 0.33 N and 0.16 N. Readouts give the drive frequency and the swing. Its read sentence: at 1 rad/s the spring's arrow is much longer than the mass's, and the swing is 0.329 m. Screen 4 asks for the swing at 2 rad/s. One choice is 1 m. Another is 0.25 m. The third is that it grows without limit. The answer is 1 m. The spring and mass arrows are both 4 N, so they cancel. That leaves the 1 N drag cωX alone to match the push, so X = 1 ÷ (0.5 × 2). Screen 5 is the main picture. The trace sits above a graph of steady swing against drive frequency. The graph runs 0 to 4 rad/s across and 0 to 1.2 m up. The same drive slider moves the push. Each setting runs the trace. Once the wobble dies, its steady swing drops a dot on the graph. A sweep drops a dot at every rate it passes. A faint line at 2 rad/s is labelled natural frequency. Its read sentence: the dots trace a hill. They climb from 0.25 m for the slowest push to about 1 m near 2 rad/s, then fall to 0.08 m at 4 rad/s. Screen 6 asks for the swing at 4 rad/s. One choice is about 0.08 m. Another is about 2 m, since a faster push gives a bigger swing. The third is 1 m, the same as at 2 rad/s. The answer is about 0.08 m, because the mass term is 16X against the spring's 4X. Screen 7 adds a damping slider from 0.5 to 6 N·s/m, in steps of 0.5. It opens at 0.5. The whole hill is drawn for the damping you set, with a ghost of the 0.5 hill. A readout gives the top of the hill and where it sits, or says there is no peak. As the damping grows, the hill drops and its top slides lower. At damping 0.5 the top is 1.01 m near 1.97 rad/s. At 1 it is 0.52 m near 1.87 rad/s. At 2 it is 0.29 m near 1.41 rad/s. From 3 there is no hill. The swing only shrinks as the push speeds up. Let go, the spring still rings at any damping below 4, critical damping. Its read sentence: at damping 2 the top of the hill is 0.29 m near 1.41 rad/s, and from damping 3 there is no hill, though the spring still rings below damping 4. Screen 8 sets damping 6 and asks where the swing is largest. One choice is at the slowest push. Another is at 2 rad/s, its natural frequency. The third is at 4 rad/s. The answer is the slowest push, about 0.24 m. Heavy drag grows with the push's speed faster than the gap between the spring and mass terms closes. Screen 9 has a switch, Spring or RLC loop. It relabels the picture as a series loop. The loop has a 1 H coil, a 0.5 Ω resistor, a 0.25 F capacitor and a 1 V AC supply. The mass becomes the coil, and the damper the resistor. The spring becomes the capacitor, and the push the supply. The capacitor's charge follows the spring's hill. As a loop, the graph plots the current's swing instead, in amps, from 0 to 2. The current is ω times the charge's swing. Its hill peaks at exactly 2 rad/s, where ωL equals 1 ÷ ωC. Readouts give the charge's swing and the current's. At 2 rad/s the charge swings 1 C and the current 2 A. That current is the supply's 1 V ÷ 0.5 Ω. Its read sentence: as a loop, the graph plots the current, which peaks at exactly 2 rad/s, where ωL equals 1 ÷ ωC. Screens 10 to 12 mix it all. Screen 10 gives a 10 V supply at 1000 rad/s, 159 Hz. It feeds 100 mH, 10 µF and 40 Ω in series. It asks for the capacitor's voltage. One choice is 25 V. Another is 10 V, since nothing can exceed the supply. The third is 4 V. The answer is 25 V. ωL and 1 ÷ ωC are both 100 Ω, so they cancel. The current is 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25 A, and 0.25 A × 100 Ω is 25 V. Screen 11 offers v = 12e^(−RCt) as the answer to dv/dt = −v ÷ RC from 12 V. It asks which check catches the mistake. One choice is the units, because RC × t is in seconds squared and an exponent must have no units. Another is the start, because it does not give 12 V at t = 0. The third is the end, because it does not fall to 0 V. The answer is the units. It does give 12 V at the start, and it does fall to 0 V. Putting it back into the rule also catches it. Screen 12 says waves near a ship's own roll rate make it roll hardest, and those rolls can capsize it. The ship rolls in waves near its own roll frequency. Bilge keels add roll damping. It asks what happens to the roll there. One choice is a smaller peak, though resonance can still occur. Another is no resonance at all. The third is the same peak, with only the start-up wobble dying sooner. The answer is a smaller peak. This straight-line equation fits only small rolls. Each puzzle offers three answers.
interactive.ignores: Time runs fast on the trace. Its 30 s plays in a few seconds. The trace always starts from rest at 0. Each dot is the settled swing worked out from the rule, not read off the trace. The spring, damper and circuit parts are ideal. The pull grows in step with the stretch, and the drag in step with the speed. Real springs can stiffen. A ship's roll is straight only at small angles. So big swings stray from this hill. The push is a pure cosine of fixed size. Real pushes, such as waves, mix many rates. The system has one way to swing. A real hull or frame has several, each with its own peak. The 1 H coil and 0.25 F capacitor are the spring's twin numbers. They are far bigger than most real parts.

explain.text:
Push a lightly damped spring or circuit back and forth, and it settles into a steady swing. That swing keeps time with the push, not with the system's own ringing. It is biggest when the push comes near the rate the system rings at by itself.

Take the same 1 kg mass, 4 N/m spring and 0.5 N·s/m damper as before. Add a 1 N push, F cos ωt. Here ω is how fast the push swings, in radians a second. The rule becomes m x″ + c x′ + k x = F cos ωt. Every term is a force, in newtons. The answer has the same shape as when the coil was switched on. It is a steady part set by the push, plus a transient set by the start. The transient is the free ringing of the unpushed spring. It dies inside an envelope whose time constant is 2m ÷ c, which is 4 s here. By 20 s, less than 1% of it is left.

The steady swing keeps the push's time, and here is why. Try a swing X cos(ωt − φ) in the rule. Here φ is how far the swing lags behind the push. Each derivative of a cosine at rate ω is a cosine at the same rate, scaled by ω. So every term swings at ω. Together they can match the push at every instant.

Now the sizes. The spring's pull is kX. The mass term is mω²X. Two derivatives of a cosine give −ω² times it, so this term points the opposite way. The damper's drag is cωX, a quarter cycle round from both. These are the three phasors of a series RLC loop. Two are opposite, and one is at right angles. They must add to F, so X = F ÷ √((k − mω²)² + (cω)²). At 1 rad/s that is 1 ÷ √(9 + 0.25), which is 0.329 m.

Now sweep the push. A slow push barely asks the mass to move. The spring takes it all, so X is near F ÷ k, 0.25 m. A fast push leaves the mass no time to follow. At 4 rad/s the mass term is 16X against the spring's 4X, and X falls to 0.08 m. In between, the spring and mass terms cancel when mω² = k. That happens at ω = √(k ÷ m) = 2 rad/s. This is the [[natural frequency]], the rate it would ring at with no damping. There, only the damper holds the push back, so X = F ÷ cω = 1 ÷ (0.5 × 2) = 1 m. A lightly damped system swings hardest when the push is near its natural frequency.[^1] That peak is [[resonance]].

Damping sets the height of the peak. At 2 rad/s the swing is F ÷ cω, so doubling the damping halves it. More damping gives a smaller peak. The top also slides lower, because the damper's share cω is smaller at lower ω. At damping 2 the top is 0.29 m near 1.41 rad/s. Heavy damping removes the hill altogether. That starts at c² = 2mk, near 2.83 N·s/m here. Past it, the damper's share grows faster than the gap between the spring and mass terms closes. So the swing only shrinks as the push speeds up. This is still short of critical damping, which is 4. So a spring that still rings can have no peak, and an overdamped spring never has one.

An AC supply on a series RLC loop gives the same equation: L q″ + R q′ + q ÷ C = V cos ωt.[^2] The capacitor's charge swings as the mass does. Its voltage is the charge ÷ C. The current is the charge's swing times ω. That extra ω moves the current's peak to exactly 1 ÷ √(LC), where ωL equals 1 ÷ ωC. That is the series resonance you already know. The capacitor's charge, and so its voltage, peaks a touch below it.

So a loop that rings when switched on can also be driven into a big swing. The capacitor's voltage can then sit far above the supply's. A ship's bilge keels add roll damping, which lowers its roll peak.[^3] This is a simplified model with ideal parts. Their pull and drag grow in step with stretch and speed. Real springs, and a ship's roll, follow it only for small swings.

**Pushed back and forth, a lightly damped spring or circuit settles to a steady swing at the push's frequency. The swing is largest when the push is near its natural frequency.**

analogy.text: A pump on rubber mounts is a mass on a spring. Its rotor is slightly out of balance, so it pushes the frame once a turn. Run it up slowly and the frame shakes hardest at one speed. Then it calms as it runs faster. That speed is near the natural frequency of the mounts. More damping in the mounts lowers the shaking there.
analogy.breaks: An out-of-balance push grows with the square of the speed, so its size is not fixed. At high speed the shake settles to a small fixed size rather than dying away. Real mounts can also rock and twist. Each way of swinging has its own peak.

practice.text:
**Safety first:** near resonance, the capacitor and the coil in a series loop can each see several times the supply voltage. Rate parts and set meters for that voltage, not the supply's.

- Name each term: what stores energy, what loses it, and what pushes.
- Check every term has the same unit: newtons for a spring, volts for a loop.
- Find the natural frequency in rad/s: √(k ÷ m) for a spring, or 1 ÷ √(LC) for a loop. Divide by 2π for hertz.
- Check the damping. The swing peaks only if c² is below 2mk. The capacitor's voltage peaks only if R² is below 2L ÷ C. A loop's current peaks at 1 ÷ √(LC), whatever R is. Critical damping is at c² = 4mk, or R² = 4L ÷ C.
- Find the steady swing at the push's frequency: X = F ÷ √((k − mω²)² + (cω)²). For a loop's current, I = V ÷ √(R² + (ωL − 1 ÷ ωC)²).
- Put the answer back into the rule. Then check its start and end values.

**Rules of thumb:** at the natural frequency the swing is F ÷ cω, so halving the damping doubles it. A very slow push gives the spring's own stretch, F ÷ k. Before you read a steady value, wait about five envelope time constants for the transient to die.

**Worked example:** a 10 V supply runs at 1000 rad/s, which is 159 Hz. It feeds 100 mH, 10 µF and 40 Ω in series. The natural frequency is 1 ÷ √(0.1 × 0.00001) = 1000 rad/s, so this is resonance. R² is 1600 Ω² and 2L ÷ C is 20000 Ω², so the damping is light. ωL = 1000 × 0.1 = 100 Ω. Likewise 1 ÷ ωC = 1 ÷ (1000 × 0.00001) = 100 Ω. They cancel, so the current is 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25 A. The capacitor sees 0.25 × 100 = 25 V. That is two and a half times the supply. Double R to 80 Ω and it falls to 12.5 V.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting an overdamped spring's swing to peak.
- Thinking a faster push always gives a bigger swing.
- Reading the start-up wobble as the steady answer.
- Thinking damping removes resonance. It lowers the peak, and a peak can remain.
- Assuming nothing in a series loop can exceed the supply voltage.
- Mixing rad/s and hertz.
